headings.title: Introduction to Parasympathomimetic (Cholinergic) Drugs
headings.content: Parasympathomimetic drugs, often called **cholinergic drugs**, are a group of medications that mimic the action of the parasympathetic nervous system. This system is responsible for our "rest and digest" activities, keeping the body calm and conserving energy. When these drugs bind to receptors in the body, they trigger responses similar to the stimulation of the vagus nerve and other parasympathetic pathways. Understanding how these agents work is vital in midwifery pharmacology because they influence critical bodily functions like smooth muscle contraction, glandular secretion, and heart rate regulation.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Action at Cholinergic Receptors
headings.content: To understand how these drugs work, we look at the two main types of cholinergic receptors: **muscarinic** and **nicotinic** receptors. Muscarinic receptors are found on smooth muscles, cardiac muscle, and glands, influencing things like pupil constriction and gut movement. Nicotinic receptors are located at autonomic ganglia and skeletal neuromuscular junctions. Cholinergic drugs either stimulate these receptors directly by mimicking acetylcholine or indirectly by preventing the enzyme **acetylcholinesterase** from breaking acetylcholine down, leaving more of it available in the synapse to prolong the effect.

headings.title: Direct versus Indirect Cholinergic Agonists
headings.content:
Cholinergic agents are broadly split into two distinct categories based on how they interact with the nervous system:

- **Direct-acting agonists**: These medications bind directly to cholinergic receptors to produce their effects. Examples include bethanechol, which helps stimulate bladder emptying.
- **Indirect-acting agonists**: These medications inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase. By stopping the breakdown of natural acetylcholine, they increase its concentration in the synaptic cleft. Examples include neostigmine, often used to reverse muscle relaxation.

headings.title: Physiological Effects on Body Systems
headings.content: Stimulating the cholinergic system creates widespread changes throughout the body. Clinicians often use the mnemonic **SLUDGE** to remember these effects: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, Gastrointestinal cramping, and Emesis. In the eyes, these drugs cause miosis, which is constriction of the pupils, and reduce intraocular pressure. On the heart, they tend to slow down the heart rate and decrease conduction velocity through the atrioventricular node.

headings.title: Key Clinical Applications in Midwifery and Obstetrics
headings.content: While not the most common class of drugs on the labor ward, cholinergic medications have specific, important roles. They are sometimes used postpartum or postoperatively to treat urinary retention when a client cannot void spontaneously after delivery or regional anesthesia. In specialized settings, indirect cholinergic agents are used to reverse the effects of non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs given during surgical procedures. Midwives must understand these uses to monitor recovery parameters effectively.

headings.title: Recognizing Cholinergic Toxicity and Side Effects
headings.content: Too much parasympathetic stimulation leads to **cholinergic toxicity** or a cholinergic crisis. This can happen from an accidental overdose of prescribed medication or exposure to certain organophosphate pesticides. The classic signs are remembered by the mnemonic **DUMBELS**: Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bronchospasm, Emesis, Lacrimation, and Salivation. Severe toxicity can cause dangerous breathing difficulties due to excessive airway secretions and bronchospasm, requiring emergency management with an anticholinergic drug like **atropine**.

headings.title: Contraindications and Nursing Considerations
headings.content: Because these drugs enhance parasympathetic activity, they can be dangerous for clients with certain underlying health problems. They are strictly contraindicated in patients with mechanical urinary or gastrointestinal obstruction, as pushing against a blocked tract can cause rupture. They are also used with great caution in individuals with asthma, because bronchospasm can be triggered. Midwives administering these agents must carefully monitor vital signs, track fluid intake and output, and ensure an antidote like atropine is readily available.
